subject: Cloud Computing
title: Client-Server: The Desktop Revolution
description: A short lesson to help you apply Client-Server: The Desktop Revolution.

hook.text: By the 1990s, every office had PCs wired to a central server down the hall.

buildup.text: The client-server model split work: desktops handled the interface, servers stored data.

discovery.text: Companies built server rooms, hired IT teams, and managed all their own hardware.

twist.text: It worked until it didn't. Servers crashed, backups failed, and scaling was a nightmare.

climax.text: Managing your own servers was expensive and risky. Companies wanted a better way.

punchline.text: Everyone wanted servers. Nobody wanted to manage them.

quiz.question: What was the main drawback of the client-server model for businesses?
options: Companies had to buy, maintain, and scale their own hardware
Client-server networks could not connect to the internet
Only government agencies were allowed to use servers

details.summary: The client-server model of the 1980s and 90s distributed computing between desktop PCs and central servers. While it decentralized processing power, it also created management headaches that would eventually drive organizations back toward centralized cloud services.
details.whyItMatters: The client-server era showed the trade-offs of distributed computing. Its management challenges directly motivated the return to centralized models through cloud computing.
takeaways: PCs and servers split computing responsibilities
Desktop management became expensive and complex
Management challenges drove the shift back to centralized cloud

faq.question: What problems did client-server create?
faq.answer: IT teams had to manage thousands of individual desktop installations, handle software compatibility issues, ensure security patches reached every machine, and support diverse hardware. The total cost of ownership for desktop PCs far exceeded the hardware price.

faq.question: How did client-server lead to cloud computing?
faq.answer: The high cost and complexity of managing distributed desktops made centralized alternatives attractive again. Web applications running in browsers eliminated client-side software management. Cloud computing completed this return to centralized, managed computing.
